senses: A European perennial alpine plant (Leontopodium alpinum), with downy leaves and small white flower heads in a dense cluster.
ety: Borrowed from German Edelweiß, from edel (“noble”) + weiß (“white”).
examples: And that will mean farewell to the edelweiss, adieu the eider goose.

senses: Female homosexuality; the state of a woman being sexually attracted to other women.
ety: From lesbian + -ism.
examples: Because all Asari present as female and use female pronouns, the deadly sexual nature of Ardat-Yakshi may reflect the continued fear of lesbianism that persists among many in human society.

senses: Capable of being pulled or stretched into thin wire by mechanical force without breaking.
Molded easily into a new form.
ety: From Old French, from Latin ductilis (“easily led”).
examples: Gold is highly ductile, allowing it to be drawn into very fine wires.
The ductile nature of copper makes it essential in electrical wiring.

senses: A tropical tree or shrub of the myrtle family, Psidium guajava.
Its yellowish tropical fruit, globular or pear-shaped with thin, yellow, green or brown skin, is often made into jams and jellies.
A medium reddish-pink color, like that of guava flesh (also called guava pink).
examples: CREAM CHEESE AND GUAVA JELLY SANDWICH: Spread an equal number of slices of lightly buttered white bread with guava jelly and cream cheese. Put slices together and trim the edges.

senses: A group of four things.
A unit of land area of two by two (that is, four) square kilometres.
A chord comprised of four notes; a tetrachord.
ety: From Ancient Greek τετράς (tetrás), analysable as tetra- + -ad.
examples: Religious movements and cults are often founded on a tetrad of elements: a prophet, a prophecy, a book, and a revelation.

senses: A pause or rest of a contemplative nature.
ety: From Biblical Hebrew סֶלָה (sélā), of unknown origin.
examples: Your crossroads moment is often a transition time, or Selah, for him as well. Two Selahs happening at once can create added stress.
Maybe this is a good time for a Selah. Lol. It is for me. Selah means “pause, and think about that” or a more literal definition, “God had spoken.”

senses: Insect-eating animal or plant.
ety: From French insectivore. In the zoological sense, coined by English philosopher and historian of science William Whewell in 1840 as an adaptation of Cuvier's coinage, French insectivore. The French terms reflect scientific New Latin origins. By surface analysis, insect + -i- + -vore.
examples: An anteater is an insectivore with a long sticky tongue to catch its prey.

senses: The position or period of rule of a chief.
The area or population ruled by a chief.
ety: From chieftain + -cy. Piecewise doublet of captaincy.
examples: At first Matenge had hated his brother because he felt the chieftaincy should be his, and this hatred drove him to overreach himself until he was discovered in a plot to assassinate his brother.
The two principles that governed my life at Mqhekezweni were chieftaincy and the Church.
And it does not help that the lowermost part of Broadway was originally laid out as a footpath by the people of the Wickquasgeck chieftaincy, long before Europeans arrived.

senses: A person who grazes cattle and/or sheep on a rural property.
The owner of a large property on which sheep or cattle graze.
ety: Inherited from Middle English grasiere, from grasen (“to graze”) + -iere (agentive suffix). By surface analysis, graze + -ier.
examples: Graziers on the tablelands are in dire straits because they do not have enough winter feed and will have to keep reducing stock.

They came ungraciously, but after his dark, bodeful hints as to the necessity of their attending service at the grazier's homestead next day, he was invited inside and a place was cleared for him at the table.

senses: a subvassal; someone holding their lands from a vassal of the crown rather than from the crown directly
ety: From Middle English vavasour, from Old French vavasour, from Medieval Latin vavassor, perhaps from vassus vassōrum (“vassal of vassals”).
examples: Fiddler’s Green is missing? That is passing strange, Lucien. He is, after all, vavasour of his own dominion. And always so… reliable.

senses: To speak or act in a manner that is intentionally ambiguous or evasive; equivocate.
ety: Borrowed from Latin praevāricātus, perfect active participle of praevāricor (“to walk crookedly; to play a false or double part”), from prae- + vāricō (“to stand with feet apart, straddle”), from vāricus (“with feet spread apart”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
examples: The people saw the politician prevaricate every day.
At the moment of her departure he could prevaricate no longer, and, confessing to the gambling, told her the truth as far as he knew it—that the guineas had been won by Wildeve.

senses: Support for the abolition of something; the tenets of abolitionists.
Support for the abolition of prisons.
Support for the abolition (banning) of sex work.
Support for the abolition (banning) of abortion.
Support for the abolition of slavery.
ety: From abolition + -ism.
examples: Abolitionism is still a powerful philosophy among contemporary feminists, both in the West and in the developing world.

senses: A ghost or spirit, often appearing in the form of a dog barking or howling through the night.
A drawn game of noughts and crosses (in Jamaica tii-taa-tuo).
ety: Jamaica, circa 18th century. From Bube dupe (“ghost”) (compare Akan adɔpe).
examples: They firmly believe in the apparition of spectres. Those of deceased friends are duppies; others, of more hostile and tremendous aspect, like our raw-head-and-bloody-bones, are called bugaboos.

No man walked alone for fear of the duppies under the trees, or the rolling calf, the ghastly animal that comes rolling towards you along the ground, its legs in chains and flames coming out of its nostrils.
Then on the left me see a duppy and try to run.

senses: A pancakelike flatbread made from fermented teff flour, a traditional food of Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia, Yemen, and the Nuer people of Sudan.
ety: Borrowed from Tigrinya እንጀራ (ʾənǧära) or Amharic እንጀራ (ʾənǧära).
examples: In Ethiopia, a volcanic pepper and spice seasoning, berbere, is widely used, and the stews called wats are eaten with a spongy flat bread, injera.
The tang of fresh injera coats the air above her head.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of dung.
Covered in dung
ety: From Middle English dongy, donky, dungy, equivalent to dung + -y. Probably a doublet of dingy.
examples: If, however, excessively dungy animals are offered for transportation, the owner of the animals is requested to clean them.

senses: Happening every minute.
Continuing; unceasing.
ety: From minute + -ly.
examples: Throwing themselves absolutely upon God's minutely providence.

senses: That sloshes or splashes.
ety: From slosh + -y.
examples: A cool schloopy-sloshy mud-cap all trickly behind his ears.

senses: That goes zoom!
Obviously characteristic of a zoom lens
ety: From zoom + -y.
examples: We play a game she calls zoomy rocket, which usually draws some nasty maternal stares.
However, the photography is at moments too poorly exposed, too zoomy, and the camera positioned too closely, for the footage to be useful

senses: The act of stipulating; a contracting or bargaining; an agreement.
Something that is stated or stipulated as a condition of an agreement.
A goal to be achieved in a chess problem; for example, to checkmate Black within a specified number of moves.
ety: Borrowed from Latin stipulātiō.
examples: The stipulations of the contract won't allow you to do that.
If I lend you my car, my only stipulation is that you fill up the gas tank before returning it.

The acts authorising the subsequent Underground lines would include a stipulation that cheap early morning fares be provided, and the Cheap Trains Act of 1883 would standardise the terms for all railways.

senses: A contribution to one's religious community or congregation of worship (notably to the LDS church).
A small part or proportion.
ety: From Middle English tithe, tythe, tethe, from Old English tēoþa, tēoða, teogoþa (in verb senses via Middle English tithen, tythen, tethen, from Old English tēoþian, teogoþian), from a proposed Proto-Germanic *tehunþô, *tehundô (“a tenth”), with its nasal consonant being lost according to the Ingvaeonic nasal spirant law. Cognate with West Frisian tsiende (“tithe”), Saterland Frisian Teeged (“tithe”), Dutch tiende, German Low German Teihnte, German Zehnt (“tithe”), Danish tiende (“tithe”), Icelandic tíund (“tithe”), Dutch tiende (“tithe”). Doublet of tenth.
examples: I scarcely know any thing that really interests me, and I would give a great deal not to be so quick-sighted as I am; it would be so pleasant to believe only a tithe of the professions that are made me.

senses: The act of presenting something for acceptance; now specifically, presenting something (e.g. a bill or cheque) for payment.
Presentation of a performance, as of a play or work of music.
The official notice (formerly required to be given in court) of the surrender of a copyhold estate.
ety: From Anglo-Norman presentment, presentement, Middle French presentement, corresponding to present + -ment.
examples: When online bill presentment, which removes all the paperwork, becomes widespread, says McKinsey's Stephenson, online banking will be far more compelling.
As to the presentment: that, by the general custom of manors, is to be made at the next court baron immediately after the surrender

senses: To cause to become less saturated or unsaturated.
To lessen the saturation of (a colour).
To decrease in saturation.
ety: From de- + saturate.
examples: With this in mind, Desai has called for imposing more stringent regulations on the ride-hailing sector, to create a more level playing field and, presumably, to desaturate the pool of drivers.

senses: To free from congestion.
ety: From de- + congest.
examples: Philip Haigh argues that the discussion in a private meeting of three options to decongest Manchester's Castlefield Corridor has reinforced a perception of 'increasing secrecy' around rail planning.

senses: A soft drink or a soda with an orange flavor.
A mixture of soda water and orange juice.
ety: From orange + -ade.
examples: The seas would turn into orangeade, deserts would blossom and glaciers melt, spring would be eternal, and wild beasts would die out or become friends of man, 'anti-lions' and 'anti-whales' to do his bidding.

senses: The sweet potato.
ety: Borrowed from Māori kūmara.
examples: They introduced the gourd, taro and kumara from the Polynesian Islands to the New Zealanders.

senses: An object (generally a post or plank on a support) set up as a target to be tilted at in jousting, or otherwise used as target practice.
ety: From Anglo-Norman quintaine, quinteine, Middle French quintaine, probably from Latin quīntāna (“street separating fifth and sixth maniples in a Roman camp”), feminine form of quīntānus (“pertaining to the fifth”).
examples: My better parts Are all thrown down; and that which here stands up Is but a quintain, a mere lifeless block.
At Offham, in Kent, tilting at the quintain provides a climax to the day's revels.
In the tiltyard, his companions felt the juddering impact of his sword-blows and saw the muscled precision of his archery and his tilting at the quintain.

senses: A (chiefly French) girl or young married woman of the lower class; especially, a young working-class woman of perceived easy morals.
The grisette amanita (Amanita vaginata), an edible mushroom in the amanita family.
A variety of low-alcohol beer that is light in body, with a noticeable tartness similar to other farmhouse ales.
ety: Borrowed from French grisette, from gris (“grey”) + -ette, named after the color of the fabric associated with low value or bad quality.
examples: The anticipations of the shopkeeper were realized, and his rooms soon became notorious through the charms of the sprightly grisette.
Oral accounts of those who remember the old grisettes say they were low-alcohol, light-bodied, saison-like golden ales of no great distinction.
She talked animatedly, with her hands, and her excitement about something as boring as the differences between a saison and a grisette was contagious.

senses: Feverish, or having a high temperature.
Full of nervous energy.
ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrīlis, from Latin febris (“fever”). By surface analysis, Latin febr- + -ile.
examples: Out in the ground, meanwhile, it was particularly disappointing to hear former England captain Andrew Strauss put the febrile atmosphere down to “people who don’t normally come to Lord’s”.
Harry Potter has become such a febrile battleground that the pattern has already become well worn.

senses: Having a pleasing shape, pleasant to look at.
ety: From Middle English schaply, schappely (“well-shaped, beautiful, attractive”), perhaps from Old English *ġesċeaplīċ (“according to design, proper, fit”) (suggested by Old English ġesċeaplīċe (“properly, fitting, well”)), equivalent to shape + -ly.
examples: The more solicitous of the two was Nurse Cramer, a shapely, pretty, sexless girl with a wholesome unattractive face.

senses: A female manager.
ety: From manager + -ess.
examples: When I worked in a toyshop, I once bought the manageress a sandwich. Do I still work there? No. Our relationship is, therefore, over. Has she given me the quid back? No.

senses: Reduced to small particles or to powder, as by crushing or pulverizing.
ety: From comminute + -ed.
examples: Hawaiian sand is utterly different: it is comminuted coral and algae, the broken detritus of a hundred thousand storms washed up against the land.

senses: The state or characteristic of being finite; limitedness.
ety: From Latin fin(is) + -itude or directly from Renaissance Latin finitūdō (“signifying a noun of state”), from fīnis (“end, limit”) + -tūdō.
examples: Matter expresses the finitude of time-space; in this world of limitation a new way of knowing becomes possible, and this way is language.
A one-car life is one of finitude and limitations.
It is our finitude and our vulnerability that keeps us open to one another and to the transcendent.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a wasp; wasplike.
Infested with wasps.
Waspish; irascible.
ety: From wasp + -y.
examples: I'm blond and blue-eyed and twenty-five, and my legs are strong and my bosom is substantial, and I have a waspy waistline.

senses: To speak or to use words to express.
ety: Partly from Middle French verbaliser and partly from verbal + -ize.
examples: Bill became tongue-tied and could not verbalize his thoughts in the presence of the girl he had a crush on.

senses: Moderation or self-restraint, especially in sexual activity; abstinence.
Uninterrupted course; continuity.
ety: Dated from the 14th century as Middle English contynence, from Old French continence, from Latin continentia (“a repression”). See also countenance.
examples: For quotations using this term, see Citations:continence.
He knew what to say; he knew also, when to leave off, — a continence which is practised by few writers.
Chastity is either abstinence or continence: abstinence is that of virgins or widows; continence of married persons.

senses: A body of elder statesmen of Japan, formerly used as informal advisors to the Emperor.
ety: From Japanese 元老 (genrō).
examples: That last part was in line with the genro Prince Saionji's advice to the Emperor: advice which the Emperor ignored.

senses: A small, snappy, belligerent mixed-breed dog; a feist dog.
Feisty behavior.
ety: Earliest sense is “fart”, and later “stink” as abbreviation for fysting cur “stinking dog” (1520s). From Middle English fysten (mid-15th century), from Old English. Cognate with Middle Dutch veest and Dutch vijst. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *fistiz (“a fart”), presumably from Proto-Indo-European *pesd-, though this is disputed. One explanation for the association of farting with small dogs is given in an 1811 slang dictionary, which suggests that the dogs were blamed for farting, specifically defining fice as “a small windy escape backwards, more obvious to the nose than ears; frequently by
examples: Sultry Joan Collins says she likes her men feisty and her beau Peter Holm is full of feist.
She looked at him, all eagerness and trust, full of feist and fun, unlike any woman he'd met before. After only a few hours, he felt as if he'd known her forever.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a blouse; loose, flowing.
ety: From blouse + -y.
examples: Here's the store where the women on televangelism programs must buy their dresses, simple, blousy, with padded shoulders, three-quarter-length sleeves, and lace collars.
Blousy tops thanks to a shipment of maternity gear from Addison's shoots help hide my faux belly from the rest of the staff, who sadly, must think I've just put on the pounds.

senses: To make moist or moister.
To become moist or moister.
ety: From moist + -en.
examples: She put on some lip balm to moisten her lips.
His eyes began to moisten as he held back tears.

senses: The act of summarizing.
The process of summarizing.
A summary; the result of summarizing.
ety: From summarize + -ation.
examples: Jim is very adept at summarization.
After summarization, these documents seem much simpler.
Jim's summarization of the incident was very useful.
